ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Phoenix, AZ
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in Phoenix, AZ for boilers, fab utility piping, tanks and structural steel. Technicians mobilize. Quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Phoenix, Arizona
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II ultrasonic technicians to Phoenix, Arizona, to measure wall thickness and examine welds on boilers, utility and process piping, storage tanks, pressure vessels and structural steel. Readings are taken to a written procedure, compared with the code or the owner's minimum, and reviewed by an ASNT NDT Level III. Reports are written for the person who has to act on them, whether that is a plant engineer, an insurer's inspector or an authorized third-party boiler agency. Request a Phoenix UT quote with your asset list and access window.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Phoenix

The Phoenix metropolitan area has been adding heavy industry quickly. Leading-edge semiconductor fabs now operate in north Phoenix and Chandler, more are under construction, and advanced packaging and chemical supply facilities have followed them to Peoria, Tempe and Casa Grande. Each of those plants depends on large utility systems: cooling water, steam, compressed air, process gases and exhaust, all in steel piping that needs thickness records and weld examination during construction and later in service. Construction of the buildings themselves, including data centers and warehouses, calls for ultrasonic examination of structural groove welds on heavy steel framing.

Elsewhere in the Valley, ultrasonic testing is applied to power generation equipment, fuel terminals and storage tanks, water and irrigation infrastructure, food and beverage plants with steam boilers, hospitals and universities with central heating plants, and highway and canal structures. Arizona's mining equipment fleet and rail operations add heavy fabricated steel that needs weld checks after repair.

Arizona's boiler regime and why UT data matters

Arizona handles boiler safety differently from many states. Since July 1, 2017, the Boiler Safety Section of the Arizona Division of Occupational Safety and Health no longer inspects boilers itself. Certificate and mandatory in-service inspections are performed by third-party agencies, either a qualified inspector from the owner's insurance carrier or an authorized contract inspector from the state's list. Power boilers above 15 psi need an annual internal certificate inspection plus an external inspection under operating conditions about six months apart, and heating and process boilers at 15 psi or less are inspected every two years. The owner is responsible for keeping the certificate current, and the state does not remind owners before a delinquent notice. See the Boiler Safety page on the Arizona Industrial Commission site for the current rules.

That means the person who reads a boiler thickness report is usually working for an insurer or a contract agency. Atlantis does not act as an inspector of record and is not a boiler inspector. We provide the ultrasonic data: shell, drum, header and tube readings at identified locations, compared with the previous campaign, with any reading near the inspector's minimum shown on the first page. Repairs to boiler pressure parts must be performed by a repair organization holding the National Board R stamp, and our weld examination is performed on request to support that work.

What ultrasonic testing measures and its limits

A transducer on the steel sends a pulse of sound and the instrument times the echo. In thickness mode, the time is converted to remaining wall using a calibrated sound velocity. In weld mode, an angled probe sends shear waves through the weld so that lack of fusion, cracks, slag and incomplete penetration return an echo. The method sees inside the metal, which makes it the standard answer for wall loss from internal corrosion or erosion and for volumetric weld quality.

Its limits are practical. The probe needs couplant and a surface smooth enough to couple. Scale, flaking paint and rough weld caps degrade readings, and the technician cleans the measuring points first. Pitted wall can give a reading from a pit shoulder rather than its floor, so the instrument may show a thicker value than the deepest pit. Cast and coarse-grained materials scatter sound. Planar flaws parallel to the beam can be missed, which is why weld procedures call for scanning at more than one angle and from both sides where possible.

Codes and acceptance criteria

Which document governs depends on the asset. Boilers and pressure vessels built to the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code use Section V for technique, with Article 4 for weld examination and Article 5 for materials; Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 covers ultrasonic examination of vessel welds. Piping under ASME B31.3 uses paragraph 344.6 and Table 341.3.2 for acceptance, and power piping falls under ASME B31.1. Structural steel is examined to AWS D1.1, which has its own ultrasonic acceptance rules for groove welds, and highway bridges to AWS D1.5. Contact thickness measurement is covered by ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 5. For in-service tanks and piping, API 653 and API 570 give the framework, and the owner's authorized inspector, not Atlantis, is responsible under those codes.

Doing UT in Phoenix heat

Heat is the defining condition. A steel pipe or tank shell in direct summer sun can be too hot to touch, and surface temperature changes the result. Sound travels at a different speed in hot steel, and plastic wedges and delay lines change even more, so a probe calibrated in a cool truck can mis-measure on hot steel. The technician calibrates on a block brought to the working temperature, uses high-temperature probes and couplant when surfaces are hot, applies a correction where the procedure requires it, and records the surface temperature on the report. Standard couplant gels run dry quickly in the dry desert air, and a drying film shows up as dropped readings, so the technician watches the signal and re-applies as needed.

Planning around the weather improves quality. Outdoor thickness surveys are best done in the early morning in summer, when metal is coolest. Monsoon season brings blowing dust and short, sharp storms, and dust on a measuring point is as bad for coupling as scale. Cooler months from autumn to spring are the easiest period for exterior tank and piping surveys.

How the work is done and who does it

Atlantis has no office in Phoenix. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, so we plan travel with the quote. They work under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, in which a Level II technician sets up, calibrates, performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT NDT Level III reviews procedures and reports. The Level III reviewer is Anoop Rayavarapu, an ASNT NDT Level III with qualifications in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If your site already has a procedure, we can work to it, and Level III consulting can review it first.

For thickness work, the technician steps a dual-element probe across a step block made from the same alloy, records the calibration, and repeats the check at the end of the shift. For welds, the setup uses an angle probe, commonly 45, 60 or 70 degrees, a reference level made from side-drilled holes, and scanning of the weld and heat-affected zone.

Weld examination in more detail

Before scanning a weld, the technician builds a reference level on a calibration block of the same thickness and acoustic properties as the part, using side-drilled holes at several depths so the instrument can compensate for beam spread. A transfer correction accounts for any difference in surface and attenuation between the block and the part. Scanning then covers the weld and a band of base metal on each side, moving the probe in a zigzag so the beam crosses the full weld volume, while the technician watches for echoes that rise above the evaluation level. Each indication is located along the weld and by depth, its length is plotted by moving the probe until the echo drops, and its amplitude is compared with the reference to judge it against the construction code.

The technician also looks at the shape of the signal. A crack or lack of fusion usually returns a sharp echo that changes quickly as the probe is moved, while slag or porosity tends to return a ragged or low echo that changes less with angle. Telling these apart takes training and judgment, which is why Level II qualification under the written practice matters and why a Level III reviews the report.

Tank and piping thickness surveys

On aboveground storage tanks in the Valley, the usual survey measures shell courses at marked vertical scan lines, with extra points at nozzles, repair patches and the bottom course, and records every reading against the original nominal plate thickness. The owner's authorized inspector uses that information under API 653 to decide remaining life and the next inspection date. On piping, readings are taken at condition monitoring locations, typically at elbows, tees, reducers and downstream of control valves where erosion and corrosion are worst, and at the same points each time so that corrosion rate can be calculated from the trend. Atlantis supplies the clean measurements; the inspector draws the conclusions.

What the UT report contains

  • Equipment identification, as it appears on the certificate or tag, with a sketch or thickness grid.
  • Procedure number and revision, governing code and acceptance table.
  • Instrument, probe, couplant, block and calibration checks, with surface temperature.
  • Technician name and level, and the Level III reviewer.
  • Readings against nominal and minimum, with the lowest values and any change from the previous campaign shown plainly.
  • For welds, each indication with position, length, depth and amplitude against the reference, and an accept or reject decision.
  • Limits: surfaces not scanned, insulated or coated areas, and any location that could not be reached.

Choosing between UT, MT and PT in Phoenix

Use ultrasonic testing for wall thickness and internal weld quality. For surface cracks in carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Phoenix is faster, and for stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys, liquid penetrant testing in Phoenix is the surface method. The national ultrasonic testing page describes the full service, NDT inspection services in Phoenix shows how the methods fit together, and the Article 5 thickness measurement guide explains the technique rules. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States; ultrasonic examination can serve as the volumetric method when your code and owner agree.

UT training for Phoenix technicians

Plants that want their own technicians can train through UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training. The Phoenix NDT training page explains the theory, simulator and employer practical, and the ultrasonic testing simulator gives trainees scanning practice before working on a real weld.

faq.q: What does Arizona require for boiler inspections and where does UT fit?
faq.a: Certificate inspections are performed by third-party agencies, either an insurer's inspector or an authorized contract inspector. Ultrasonic thickness readings give that inspector wall data, while the inspector, not the NDE technician, decides on the certificate.

faq.q: Can you do ultrasonic thickness testing on a hot surface in Phoenix?
faq.a: Yes, with high-temperature probes and couplant, calibration on a block at working temperature, and a recorded surface temperature. Very hot surfaces may need cooling or a different time of day before readings are reliable.

faq.q: Why does summer heat affect ultrasonic readings?
faq.a: Sound velocity changes with temperature in steel and even more in plastic wedges, so a cool calibration gives errors on hot metal. The procedure calibrates at working temperature and corrects readings where needed.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on a Phoenix weld?
faq.a: In some cases. Several codes carry ultrasonic provisions, and ASME Section VIII allows it only under specific conditions. The owner, engineer and authorized inspector must agree before the work starts.

faq.q: What codes cover ultrasonic examination of structural welds in Arizona?
faq.a: AWS D1.1 covers structural steel and AWS D1.5 covers highway bridges, with acceptance criteria for ultrasonic examination of groove welds. The contract documents and owner specification add requirements, so we work from those.

faq.q: Does dust or monsoon weather affect UT in Phoenix?
faq.a: Yes. Dust blocks coupling and storms interrupt outdoor work. Crews clean the measuring points, protect the instrument and reschedule outdoor thickness surveys around monsoon weather where possible.

faq.q: Is Atlantis an authorized boiler inspection agency in Arizona?
faq.a: No. Atlantis is not a boiler inspection agency and does not sign as inspector of record. We perform ultrasonic examination and supply data to the owner's authorized inspector or insurer.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Phoenix?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Phoenix, so crews travel in from outside the Valley and the trip is built into your quote. Enquiries receive a reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can you measure thickness through coatings or insulation?
faq.a: Insulation has to be opened at each reading point. Coatings may be measured through when the technique is verified for them, and the procedure states whether the coating is removed or read through.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Phoenix, AZ | MT Testing
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Phoenix, AZ for structural steel, cranes, heavy equipment and pressure parts. Technicians travel to your site. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Phoenix, Arizona
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends magnetic particle technicians to Phoenix, Arizona, to find surface and near-surface cracks in welds, castings, forgings and in-service steel. Typical scopes are structural steel erection welds, crane and lifting gear, heavy equipment frames, pressure equipment repairs and fabricated assemblies. The examination follows a written procedure and the report is reviewed by an ASNT NDT Level III. Ask for a Phoenix magnetic particle quote and tell us the parts, the code and the access.

Where mag particle testing is used in Phoenix

Construction is the largest driver. The Valley has seen large semiconductor fabs, advanced packaging plants, data centers and warehouses go up, and each building rests on heavy structural steel with field welds at columns, beams, braces and connection plates. Crane lifts, lifting lugs and rigging attachments used during erection are examined too. Heavy fabricators in the metro area build tanks, trailers, support frames and plate assemblies, and the examination of weld toes, gouged repairs and attachments is routine before shipment.

Arizona's mines and aggregate plants, rail lines and truck fleets add equipment frames, buckets, booms and drive components that crack in service. Power plants, water facilities and fuel terminals have vessels, supports and piping attachments that are checked at outages. Whenever carbon or low-alloy steel is welded, repaired or cyclically loaded, mag particle testing is the quickest way to prove the surface is free of cracks.

What the method finds and what it misses

The method works only on ferromagnetic steel. A part that is carbon steel, low-alloy steel or a martensitic stainless grade can be magnetized; austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys cannot, and they need penetrant testing instead. When flux passes through a magnetized part and meets a crack, some of it leaks out of the surface and holds fine iron particles in a visible line. Surface-breaking cracks, laps, seams and toe cracks show up sharply, and flaws just under the surface can appear as a softer, broader line.

Limits matter. The sensitivity drops quickly with depth, so internal flaws are not found. Cracks parallel to the field barely show, so a second examination at about ninety degrees is required. Thick paint, scale and spatter reduce sensitivity and have to be removed. Geometry features such as sharp corners, keyways and changes in section create non-relevant indications that the technician must recognize and resolve, and a weld-to-base metal permeability difference can create misleading marks at the weld toe.

Codes and acceptance criteria

The technique comes from ASME Section V Article 7, and the acceptance criteria are those of the construction code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 covers pressure vessel welds, and ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 with Table 341.3.2 covers process piping. Structural steel and cranes are examined to AWS D1.1, and bridges to AWS D1.5. ASTM E709 is the guide for the method and ASTM E1444 is the practice. Repairs to boilers and pressure vessels fall under the National Board Inspection Code, and in Arizona such repairs must be done by an organization holding the National Board R stamp. Boiler certificate inspections in the state are carried out by third-party agencies, as set out on the Arizona Boiler Safety page. Atlantis performs the examination and reports the indications; it does not act as the inspector who accepts the repair.

Technique in the field and the shop

Field work usually uses an electromagnetic yoke. Under ASME Section V Article 7, an alternating-current yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, and a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, so the technician proves the lift with a test weight before use. The weld and the adjoining base metal are cleaned, the yoke is placed across the weld, particles are applied, and the examination is repeated with the yoke turned about ninety degrees. Prods are only used when the code permits and the surface can tolerate arcing.

Dry powder is applied with a hand bulb in a color that contrasts with the steel, and in Phoenix's dry air it adheres well and builds a clear indication. Wind is the enemy, since it blows powder off the weld, so a windbreak or a lower-wind time of day is used. Wet particles in a liquid carrier give a stronger response on fine cracks. Fluorescent particles need UV-A light and a dark area, and in the strong Arizona sun that means a tent or a shaded enclosure. After examination, parts may be demagnetized, and the residual field is checked with a gauss meter.

Heat, sun and dust

Phoenix heat shapes magnetic particle work. Steel in direct sun can exceed the temperature the particle suspension or the dry powder can tolerate. Liquid carriers evaporate rapidly and oil-based carriers become a flammability concern on hot steel, so the procedure sets a surface temperature ceiling and the technician checks it with a contact thermometer. Hot parts can be shaded or allowed to cool, and the work moved to early morning. Dry powder tends to stick to hot steel in clumps. Dust is the second condition: windblown dust settles on cleaned surfaces and becomes a background that obscures small indications, so the surface is cleaned just before the examination, not hours earlier.

Who performs and reviews the work

Atlantis has no office in Phoenix, so crews are mobilized from outside the Valley for the scope you agree. They work under the company's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. The Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, who is qualified in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT at ASNT Level III. If your site has its own written practice, we can work to it, and our written practice development service can help draft one. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

Typical Phoenix scopes in practice

A structural erection scope usually lists the welds by connection type: column splices, beam flange welds, brace gusset plates and base plate attachments. The specification states a percentage of welds to be examined, and the technician works through them with a yoke, marking each weld that has been examined and recording any indication on a map. A crane or lifting scope focuses on load-bearing welds, pin bosses, hook blocks and shackle eyes, with the load rating documents guiding which areas are critical. For heavy equipment such as truck frames, buckets and booms, the technician follows the known fatigue paths: welds at corners, gussets and pin bores, and the heat-affected zone of previous repairs. Each of these jobs starts with cleaning, because a weld coated in grease and dust will not give a clear result.

Preparing for the visit

A few questions answered in advance make a Phoenix visit efficient. Which surfaces are painted, and may the coating be removed, or is the paint thin enough to examine through? Is electrical power available at the work location for a bench or a yoke, and what is the extension cord distance? Is there shade, or must the crew bring a canopy? Will scaffolds or lifts be ready before the technician arrives, and what safety orientation is required at the site gate? Do the drawings show which welds are to be examined and to which acceptance table? A quick exchange of photographs usually settles all of this and lets the crew bring the right yoke, powder color, and cleaning supplies for one trip.

Judging indications and the repair loop

Each mark is first sorted as relevant or non-relevant. Relevant indications come from real discontinuities; non-relevant ones come from a change in section or a magnetic writing mark, and the technician proves which it is by cleaning and re-testing. Under ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6, an indication longer than three times its width is linear, and linear indications in a finished weld are generally unacceptable. When a crack is found, the ends are marked, it is ground out under the owner's repair procedure, and the ground area is re-examined before welding. The repaired weld is then examined once more by the same method, and each step is recorded.

What the MT report shows

  • Part or weld identification, material and surface condition.
  • Procedure number and revision, code and acceptance criteria.
  • Yoke or bench, lifting power check, particle type, carrier and lighting measurements.
  • Surface temperature at the time of the examination.
  • Technician name and level, and the Level III reviewer.
  • Each indication by location, orientation and length, with a photograph and an accept or reject decision.
  • Demagnetization status and residual field reading.
  • Areas that could not be covered.

Choosing between MT, PT and UT in Phoenix

For carbon and low-alloy steel with a surface-crack question, mag particle testing is the first choice. Where the steel is stainless or aluminum, turn to liquid penetrant testing in Phoenix. When the question is thickness or internal weld quality, use ultrasonic testing in Phoenix. NDT inspection services in Phoenix shows how these fit together. The national magnetic particle testing page and the magnetic particle testing guide provide background. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States.

MT training for Phoenix teams

If you want in-house capability, see MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and the NDT training page for Phoenix, which explains how the course, simulator work and hands-on practical at your facility fit your written practice.

faq.q: When is magnetic particle inspection the right choice in Phoenix?
faq.a: It suits carbon and low-alloy steel where the concern is surface or near-surface cracking, such as structural welds, crane steel, equipment frames and weld repairs. It is fast and sensitive for those materials.

faq.q: Can mag particle testing be used on stainless steel or aluminum?
faq.a: Not on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum or copper alloys, because they are not magnetic. Liquid penetrant testing is used for surface-breaking flaws on those materials.

faq.q: How does Phoenix heat affect magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Hot steel can exceed what the particles or carrier tolerate, and liquid carriers evaporate quickly. The technician measures surface temperature, shades or cools the part, or moves the work to a cooler hour, following the procedure.

faq.q: Can you do fluorescent MT outdoors in Arizona?
faq.a: Fluorescent particles need UV-A light and a darkened area, so in bright sun the technician uses a tent or enclosure. Without enough darkness, visible particles are the alternative if the procedure allows it.

faq.q: Why are two directions of magnetization required?
faq.a: A crack that runs along the direction of the field leaks almost no flux, so it can stay invisible. A second pass at about ninety degrees makes sure cracks in any orientation can be found.

faq.q: Does wind or dust affect dry powder testing?
faq.a: Yes. Wind can blow powder away from the weld and dust adds background that hides small indications. Windbreaks, cleaning just before testing, and choosing calmer hours address both problems.

faq.q: What does Arizona require for repairs of boilers and pressure vessels?
faq.a: Repairs must be performed by an organization holding the National Board R stamp, and boiler certificate inspections are done by third-party agencies. Our MT results support the repair record but do not replace the inspector.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Phoenix?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Phoenix. Crews travel in from outside the area, and we build that travel into the quote before you commit. We reply to every enquiry within one business day.

faq.q: Can you examine structural steel erection welds in Phoenix?
faq.a: Yes. Field welds on columns, beams and connection plates, plus lifting lugs, can be examined to AWS D1.1 or the project specification. Send the specification and the weld list so the scope matches.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Phoenix, AZ | Dye Penetrant
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection in Phoenix, AZ for stainless piping, aluminum parts, tanks, welds and castings, with heat-ready procedures. Technicians mobilize.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Phoenix, Arizona
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to Phoenix, Arizona, for liquid penetrant testing of welds and parts where magnetic methods cannot be used: stainless steel process piping and vessels, aluminum and nickel-alloy components, castings and machined parts. Every examination follows a written procedure that accounts for Phoenix heat, and the report is reviewed by an ASNT NDT Level III. Request a Phoenix penetrant testing quote with the material, surface condition and code.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Phoenix

Greater Phoenix has a concentration of semiconductor manufacturing, and the plants around it depend on stainless steel gas, chemical and water systems. Welds on those lines are often examined by visual and, where the owner permits, by penetrant testing, with the owner's own rules on what may touch wetted surfaces. Advanced packaging and chemical supply facilities, laboratories, hospitals and food and beverage plants add stainless tanks and sanitary piping. Aerospace and defense suppliers in the metro area work with aluminum, titanium and nickel parts, and machine shops and repair facilities check cast and machined components for cracks.

Power, water and fuel facilities contribute non-magnetic and alloy components too, such as stainless instrumentation lines, bronze valves, aluminum structures and weld overlay. In all of these, penetrant testing finds the tight surface cracks that are hard to see with the eye alone.

What penetrant testing finds and what it cannot

The method finds only flaws open to the surface. A thin liquid is drawn into a crack, pore or lap by capillary action. Excess is removed and a developer pulls the trapped liquid back to the surface where it shows as a visible or fluorescent mark. Because the method does not rely on magnetism, it works on stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys and ceramics as well as steel, and on any non-porous surface.

Its weakness is that anything covering a crack mouth defeats it. Smeared metal from grinding or machining, paint, oil, scale, flux and dried cleaner can all seal a flaw. Rough, porous surfaces hold penetrant and create background that hides indications. Flaws below the surface are invisible to the method, so internal weld quality needs ultrasonic testing, which means the choice of method matters at the planning stage.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 6 sets the technique rules, and the acceptance criteria come from the construction code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 covers pressure vessel welds, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 cover process piping, and AWS D1.1 and D1.6 cover structural and stainless welds. ASTM E165 is the general-industry practice and ASTM E1417 sets the practice and performance checks for penetrant materials. When the base metal is austenitic stainless steel or a nickel alloy, the procedure restricts the halogen and sulfur content of the penetrant, remover and developer, because residues can cause corrosion or cracking later.

Boiler repairs in Arizona follow the National Board Inspection Code and must be carried out by an organization holding the R stamp, with certificate inspections performed by third-party agencies, as described on the Arizona Boiler Safety page. Atlantis reports penetrant indications against the code's acceptance criteria; the responsible inspector accepts the repair.

The temperature problem in Phoenix

Penetrant materials are designed to work in a narrow window. ASME Section V Article 6 treats 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit as the standard range for both the part and the materials. Phoenix summers push sunlit steel and aluminum far above that. Hot metal flashes the solvent off the penetrant before it can enter a tight crack, bakes excess penetrant into a stain that resists removal, and makes the developer dry unevenly. Nothing looks wrong on the day. The flaw simply does not show.

The Article allows a procedure to be qualified for a temperature outside the standard range by processing a comparator block at that temperature and comparing it with one processed in the standard range. That is the route when a part cannot be cooled. More often the answer is simpler: examine early in the day, shade the part, let it cool, and check the surface with a contact thermometer before applying penetrant and again afterward. Aerosol cans left in a closed vehicle exceed their labelled temperature in an Arizona summer, so they are kept in a cooler. Winter nights and mornings occasionally fall near the lower limit, and the same check applies.

Cleaning and drying in dry air

Low humidity changes the cleaning step. Solvent cleaner flashes off almost at once, which speeds drying but tempts a technician to over-wipe, and an over-wetted cloth can pull penetrant out of shallow cracks. Fine desert dust lodges in surface openings and blocks entry, so cleaning is done immediately before penetrant is applied, not earlier. After the dwell time, excess is removed with lightly dampened cloths in one direction, and developer is applied in a thin, even coat. In the dry air, developing time is short, and the technician looks at the part during development, not only at the end.

Choosing the penetrant system

Penetrant materials are classified by type and method. Type I penetrants are fluorescent and viewed under UV-A light, while Type II penetrants are visible dye. The removal method is water washable, post-emulsifiable or solvent removable, and each has its own sensitivity and handling needs. For field work in Phoenix the usual choice is a solvent-removable visible system, because it is portable and needs no water supply, with a fluorescent system reserved for critical welds or fine cracks and a tent or dark room to make it work in daylight. The procedure names the exact materials, and materials from different manufacturers are never mixed within one examination.

Typical Phoenix scopes

A stainless piping scope usually names the lines and welds to be examined, the cleanliness requirement and the acceptance table. A weld repair scope names the area ground out and the sequence: examine after grinding, weld, then examine again. Aluminum parts scopes list the components and finish, because anodized or coated surfaces need to be handled differently from bare metal. Cast components such as valve bodies and pump casings are examined after machining to find shrinkage and cracks open to the surface. For each job we ask for photographs, the drawing and the specification, and for the temperature expected at the work location during the visit.

Preparation and the repair loop

Preparation takes more of the time than the penetrant itself. The technician removes paint, scale and spatter, degreases the area, lets it dry fully, and checks the temperature. After the examination, any crack is marked and ground out under the owner's repair procedure. The ground area is examined again before welding to confirm the flaw is gone, and the finished repair is examined a final time. Parts are cleaned afterward so residue does not interfere with later welding, coating or service. Each step is recorded so the owner holds a complete trail.

Process piping and restricted-contact systems

Owners of high-purity and semiconductor systems often restrict which materials may touch wetted surfaces, because residues can contaminate a process. Some specify visual examination with a borescope or ultrasonic testing instead of penetrant. Before a penetrant job on that kind of system, the technician asks for the owner's cleanliness requirements and agrees which surfaces may be examined, which cleaners are approved and how post-cleaning is verified. Sometimes the answer is that penetrant is not the right method, and we say so.

Who performs and reviews the work

Atlantis has no office in Phoenix, so technicians travel to your site from elsewhere and the plan is set with you in the quote. They work under the company's written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, in which a Level II technician performs and interprets the examination and an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. That reviewer is Anoop Rayavarapu, who holds ASNT NDT Level III qualifications in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. We can work to your site's procedure and can help write or qualify one through Level III consulting. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

What the PT report shows

  • Identification of the part, weld or area, with a sketch where useful.
  • Material, surface condition and measured surface temperature, before and after.
  • Procedure number and revision, penetrant type and method, remover and developer, with batch numbers.
  • Dwell and developing times and the lighting used.
  • Technician name and level, and the Level III reviewer.
  • Each indication with position and size, and the accept or reject decision.
  • Areas not examined and the post-cleaning performed.

Choosing between PT, MT and UT in Phoenix

Choose penetrant testing for non-magnetic metals and for surface cracks in any non-porous material. For carbon steel where speed matters, magnetic particle inspection in Phoenix is faster, and for thickness or internal weld quality, ultrasonic testing in Phoenix is the right method. NDT inspection services in Phoenix shows how the methods combine. The national penetrant testing page covers the service generally, and ASME Section V Article 6 explained goes through the technique rules. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States.

PT training for Phoenix teams

If you want in-house capability, see PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, practice on the penetrant testing simulator, and read the Phoenix NDT training page for how the pieces fit your written practice.

faq.q: What is dye penetrant testing used for in Phoenix?
faq.a: It finds surface-breaking cracks, laps and porosity on non-porous material. In Phoenix that includes stainless piping and tanks, aluminum and nickel-alloy parts, castings, machined components and weld repairs.

faq.q: How does Phoenix heat affect penetrant testing?
faq.a: Sunlit metal can exceed the 125 degree Fahrenheit upper limit of the standard range, so penetrant dries too fast and developer goes on unevenly. Crews examine early, shade or cool the part, or use a qualified high-temperature technique.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be done on a part hotter than the standard range?
faq.a: Yes, if the procedure is qualified for that temperature using a comparator block processed at the intended temperature and compared with one processed in the standard range. Otherwise the part should be cooled.

faq.q: Can penetrant find cracks below the surface?
faq.a: No. The liquid has to enter the flaw from the surface, so subsurface flaws are not detected. Ultrasonic testing is the usual method for internal weld quality where the code allows.

faq.q: Why is penetrant sometimes restricted on semiconductor and high-purity systems?
faq.a: Residues from penetrant, remover and developer could contaminate a process, so owners may restrict what touches wetted surfaces. We confirm the owner's cleanliness rules first and recommend another method if penetrant is not suitable.

faq.q: Why are halogens and sulfur limited for stainless steel?
faq.a: Residues containing those elements can promote corrosion or cracking on austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys, so procedures require low-halogen, low-sulfur materials and thorough post-cleaning on those alloys.

faq.q: Does desert dust affect penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. Dust can lodge in surface openings and block penetrant entry, so the surface is cleaned just before penetrant is applied and wind protection is used when needed.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Phoenix?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Phoenix. Crews are mobilized from outside the Valley once the scope is agreed, and travel is part of the quote. We reply to enquiries within one business day.

faq.q: Do you examine aluminum and titanium parts with penetrant?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the procedure, the material compatibility and the acceptance criteria are agreed in advance. Aluminum smears easily, so cleaning and sometimes light etching are specified before penetrant is applied.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing Phoenix, AZ | UT & Level III Review
rt.description: Looking for radiographic testing in Phoenix, AZ? Atlantis does not perform RT in the US. Explore UT as an alternative and Level III radiograph review.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Phoenix, Arizona: What Atlantis Does and Does Not Do
rt.html:
Atlantis NDT does not perform industrial radiography anywhere in the United States, with film or with digital detectors. Industrial radiography uses sealed gamma sources or X-ray machines, and in this country it is licensed activity governed by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission under 10 CFR Part 34 or by the equivalent rules of an Agreement State. Arizona is an Agreement State, so radiography there is licensed through the state's own radiation regulatory agency. Atlantis does not hold a radiography licence for work in Phoenix and does not offer the service, so we do not shoot or expose radiographs for any weld, casting or pipe.

What you can do instead

If your Phoenix project specification calls for radiography, you may still have useful options with us. They keep your acceptance decisions, procedures and records on a solid footing, whichever contractor handles any required exposures.

Ultrasonic testing as a volumetric alternative

For many welds in piping, vessels and structural steel, ultrasonic examination can serve as the volumetric method in place of radiography. Both ASME B31.3 and API 1104 permit ultrasonic examination of production welds under their own provisions, and AWS D1.1 gives acceptance criteria of its own for ultrasonic examination of groove welds. ASME Section VIII Division 1 allows ultrasonic examination to replace radiography only under specific conditions in the Code, and not every joint qualifies. Ultrasonic examination detects planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks with good reliability, and it needs no exclusion zone, which in busy Phoenix construction sites, with many trades working at once, can save considerable disruption.

The substitution must be agreed beforehand with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector, and written into the procedure. See ultrasonic testing in Phoenix for how weld examination and thickness surveys are carried out, including how technicians handle summer heat.

Independent Level III review of radiographs

Reviewing existing radiographic work needs no radiation licence, because it relies on images and records. Anoop Rayavarapu, an ASNT NDT Level III with qualifications in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, can review radiographs in film or digital image form against ASME Section V Article 2 and your construction code. That covers a second read of borderline or disputed indications, a check of the technique sheet, image quality indicators, density and sensitivity, and review of an RT contractor's procedure and written practice before work starts. The purpose is to tell the owner whether the images support the accept or reject decision.

This forms part of our Level III consulting. It helps when a fabricator and an owner disagree about a weld, when records are inherited from an earlier contractor, or when a quality manager wants an independent opinion before releasing a package.

Radiography theory training and other methods

For teams that want to understand radiography, the radiographic testing Level 2 course covers principles, techniques, interpretation and code acceptance. Radiation safety training and licensing are separate matters between the employer and the regulator. For Phoenix teams, the NDT training page for Phoenix explains the pieces together. For surface work on steel, see magnetic particle inspection in Phoenix, and for stainless steel and aluminum see penetrant testing in Phoenix. The wider picture is at NDT inspection services in Phoenix. Atlantis has no office in Phoenix and technicians are mobilized to your site. Describe your weld and code and we will say honestly whether UT or a Level III review can help.

faq.q: Is radiography available from Atlantis in Phoenix, Arizona?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under NRC rules or those of an Agreement State such as Arizona, and Atlantis does not offer it.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my Phoenix weld?
faq.a: Sometimes, when the construction code allows it and the owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree beforehand. Substitution under Section VIII is limited to specific conditions, while other codes have their own ultrasonic provisions.

faq.q: Can Atlantis review radiographs from another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT NDT Level III can review film or digital images and technique records against ASME Section V Article 2 and your code. This is a records review and needs no radiation licence.

faq.q: Do you name or recommend radiography contractors in Phoenix?
faq.a: No. If your scope needs exposures, select a licensed provider through your own procurement. We can review that provider's procedure and images independently if you want a second opinion.

faq.q: Do you teach radiographic testing?
faq.a: Our Level 2 radiographic testing course covers theory, how to read images and how codes judge them. Radiation safety licensing stays separate, and certification belongs to the employer under its written practice.
